references.text: Hosea emphasizes that God desires mercy and not sacrifice, pointing to Jesus' call to sinners rather than the self-righteous.
God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but wants them to turn from their ways and live. This reflects Jesus' purpose in calling sinners to repentance.
Isaiah calls the wicked to leave their ways and turn to the Lord, who will show mercy. This parallels Jesus' call to sinners.
The Lord invites reconciliation and offers forgiveness even for serious sins, which aligns with Jesus' mission of calling sinners to repentance.
The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus says he has not come to call the righteous, but sinners.
The parallel passage in Mark where Jesus explains that it is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick, and that he has come to call sinners.
Jesus says there is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who do not need repentance—this expands on his purpose of calling sinners.
Jesus states that the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost, summarizing this same call to sinners.
Paul confirms that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, directly reflecting Jesus' own words in Luke 5:32.
The Lord desires all people to come to repentance, supporting Jesus' purpose of calling sinners to turn from their ways.
God now commands all people everywhere to repent. This underscores the universal call to repentance that Jesus came to bring.
The preceding verse where Jesus uses the image of a doctor who has not come for the healthy but for the sick, forming the basis for his statement about calling sinners.
